title: Pro Football Focus details Texas A&M QB's successful 2026 debut
description: PFF provided Texas A&M QB Marcel Reed's day through the air on Saturday, detailing his deep throw grade and improved decision making when pressured.
fullText:
Texas A&M opened the 2026 regular season in dominant fashion, at least in the second half, blowing out Missouri State 50-0 on Saturday night thanks to an elite defensive effort combined with 236 rushing yards and six touchdowns, while redshirt junior quarterback Marcel Reed was highly impressive, completing 21/30 for 233 yards and 2 touchdowns, and a 75.9 QBR.

Per Pro Football Focus, Reed led all Texas A&M players with an 80.6 offensive grade and 78.6 passing grade, which, compared to last year's season opener, is a marginal improvement, especially based on PFF standards for quarterback grading. Looking poised in the pocket and delivering several NFL-level throws, Reed's offseason focus on fixing his mechanical issues resulted in his best preseason, confirmed by coach Mike Elko last week.

Some of Reed's best throws came behind the line of scrimmage and on 20-plus-yard deep throws, directing his receiver upfield on swing passes, while connecting with transfer wide receiver Isaiah Horton on multiple deep throws that showed off his improved accuracy and touch.

PFF released its Passing Pressure, Concept & Direction Report after Saturday's win, providing more context regarding Reed's success at every level of the field. According to the site, Reed was highly successful in play action, earning an elite 91.0 passing grade, while finishing 16/16 on behind-the-LOS and short throws and 4/7 on intermediate attempts.

When blitzed, Reed earned a solid 78.0 passing grade, making quick decisions to check down to the flat or use his legs to prevent a negative play. This version of Marcel Reed, combined with the offensive line continuing to improve, gives the Aggies a legitimate shot at returning to the CFP and competing in every SEC game at home or on the road.

title: 'They're going to protect me': Texas A&M QB Marcel Reed praises O-line
description: Texas A&M QB Marcel Reed heaped praise on his O-line despite the unit's early struggles, sharing a close relationship with several starters.
fullText:
Texas A&M's offensive line struggled during the first half of Saturday's 50-0 shutout win over Missouri State, but improved in the second half, much to starting quarterback Marcel Reed's liking, as third-year coach Mike Elko and OL coach Adam Cushing made the necessary adjustments, leading to better communication at the LOS while paying close attention to their assignments.

At left tackle, LSU transfer Tyree Adams earned the third-highest Pro Football Focus grade (79.3) and was highly impressive in pass protection and run blocking, which is very important heading into Saturday's home matchup vs. Arizona State, while junior left guard Blake Ivy should retain his starting job, as his first-half struggles disappeared after halftime.

These blocking issues, after watching the tape a second time, stemmed from missed assignments, which was expected in the first game of the season after replacing four starters from the 2025 unit. Depth-wise, Elko could have certainly made drastic changes, but chose to stick with most of his original starting rotation, including South Carolina transfer right guard Trovon Baugh, who also struggled.

After the game, Marcel Reed discussed his close relationship with all his offensive linemen, including right tackle Wilkin Formby, Tyree Adams, and Blake Ivy, whose bond should help this revamped group protect their quarterback and play much better football for the rest of the season.

"I remember running out, and Wilkin Formby just said, 'I love you, brother.' I said, 'I love you, too.' Tyree Adams was checking in on me. I saw Blake Ivy maul somebody and get hype. They're going to protect me."

Mentality is everything as an offensive lineman, knowing that your central job is to keep the quarterback clean and open up holes in the running game. It's up to Adam Cushing to do his job and fix these remaining issues, which could lead to a change in the lineup, but right now, the second-half improvement shows this group is poised to improve.

"They said more to me. They tried to lift me up. Respect those guys a lot and the care they have for their quarterbacks. Those guys want to protect. I know they will get it done each Saturday."

Texas A&M will host Arizona State on Saturday, Sept. 6, which will air on ABC at 11 a.m.

title: Born here but deported. A Texas man's harrowing ordeal.
description: A traffic stop in Texas landed Brian Morales García, a U.S. citizen, in immigration custody. After he was deported to Mexico, a lawsuit helped bring him back.
fullText:
Brian José Morales García was riding beside his boss through the Texas Hill Country, bound for an air-conditioning job near Fredericksburg, when a state trooper stopped their pickup truck.

Over the next four days, the 25-year-old was shuttled through a succession of detention facilities. Along the way, his attorney said, he was stripped, shoved and threatened with years in prison. By April 7, he was aboard a deportation flight to Mexico.

The country sending him away was his own.

Morales García was born in Denver, according to a copy of his birth certificate reviewed by USA TODAY.

He is part of a long, largely uncounted history of U.S. citizens swallowed by the nation's immigration system. The federal government does not release data on how often its agents detain or deport U.S. citizens, but investigations by journalists, researchers and oversight agencies have documented thousands of citizens detained, deported or otherwise targeted by immigration authorities across decades. One study estimated that U.S. citizens account for as many as 1.5% of all deportees.

A Government Accountability Office report from 2021 offers one glimpse of how often Americans may become entangled in immigration enforcement. Between fiscal year 2015 and the first two quarters of fiscal year 2020, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 674 potential U.S. citizens, detained 121 and deported 70, according to the report. The majority of those deportations — 66 people — occurred during President Donald Trump's first term.

Yet, even those numbers do not tell the full story. The watchdog agency found that ICE did not consistently track cases involving potential U.S. citizens, making it impossible to know how many people were actually swept into the system.

The problem has persisted through successive Republican and Democratic administrations. Now, experts fear a persistent failure is colliding with a rapid expansion of immigration enforcement — one pushed to deliver record numbers of arrests, increasingly aided by state and local police and operating with fewer internal checks. The result, they warn, is that more citizens could be swept into the dragnet and have fewer places to turn once they are.

"This is a system that is advancing with less accountability now than before," said Jacqueline Stevens, a political science professor at Northwestern University and founder of the school's Deportation Research Clinic. "And less oversight because they're not producing the records that they should be producing on these cases."

Citizens represent a sliver of those targeted by immigration authorities. But for those who are wrongfully detained or deported, the experience can leave lasting trauma, mounting legal costs and consequences that take years to resolve.

For Morales García, returning home required a federal lawsuit — and nearly five months outside his own country.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to USA TODAY's requests for comment. The Department of Justice declined to comment on Morales García's case, citing pending litigation. In court filings, however, the government said Morales García told federal agents he was born in Mexico and freely chose to return there.

In 2001, Morales García was born in Denver to two young Mexican parents who had come to the United States in search of better opportunities. Later that year, he was baptized at St. Therese Catholic Church in Aurora, Colorado, where a baptismal record lists Denver as his birthplace. Morales García also has a Social Security card, a copy of which USA TODAY reviewed. Like cards issued to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, his bears no restriction requiring DHS authorization to work.

But the family's life in the United States was brief. After Morales García's younger brother was born in 2002, his parents returned to Mexico to raise their sons close to family, said his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. Morales García would spend most of the next two decades there, growing up speaking Spanish and eventually getting married.

As he prepared to become a father, Morales García returned to the United States to find work and support his growing family in Mexico, including his wife who was pregnant with their first daughter. He drove north from Aguascalientes — a sunbaked city in Mexico's central highlands — in January 2025. At the port of entry, Morales García showed a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer his Colorado birth certificate, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. The officer let him through.

He settled in Austin, moving through a series of construction jobs before landing one installing air-conditioning units.

On April 3, he was riding to one of those jobs when Texas Department of Public Safety troopers stopped his employer's pickup near Fredericksburg for an alleged window tint violation, according to the federal lawsuit his attorneys later filed. No one in the truck received a citation as a result of the stop, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Morales García repeatedly told the state troopers — and, later, the Gillespie County sheriff's deputies who were called in to translate — that he is American. He explained in Spanish that he had been born in Denver and asked for an opportunity to retrieve his documents, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

The officers, however, contacted ICE. The agency instructed them to hold Morales García and another passenger, according to the lawsuit, and Morales García was booked into the Gillespie County Jail. Both Texas DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff's Office have formal partnerships with ICE, part of a growing network of state and local agencies enlisted to help enforce federal immigration law.

"There's no law in this country that says that U.S. citizens have to have ID on them when they're going out or riding as passengers in a car," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "What's happening in the streets is that DPS, ICE and all the sheriffs are just stopping people with brown skin and asking them what their status is, and if they don't have an answer that they like, they're taking them. And it's quiet and it's silent what they're doing, but it's a slippery slope."

Morales García was ultimately transferred into CBP custody. There, Lincoln-Goldfinch said, agents ridiculed his repeated claims that he was American and warned that, if he continued making them, he could face as many as five years in prison.

"At that point, he'd been abused for four days straight, and he believed that he was going to either sign the paperwork they told him to sign or go to jail for years," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "So he signed these documents... under duress."

With his signature, Morales García had agreed to be deported to Mexico.

Morales García's ordeal fits a pattern Stevens, the political scientist, has spent decades tracing. Some people discover only after they are detained that they have a claim to U.S. citizenship. Others, like Morales García, know they are American from the beginning, yet watch as officers dismiss their claims and the deportation process moves forward anyway.

Stevens calls these cases "the 900-pound gorilla in the coal mine."

"I study U.S. citizens not because I care more about U.S. citizens being wrongfully deported than anybody else," she said. "But if even U.S. citizens can't survive the lawlessness of the deportation process, that tells us a lot about what's happening to everybody else."

Claims of citizenship are supposed to interrupt the machinery of deportation. Federal regulations require unresolved claims to be referred to immigration court. ICE policy also requires officers to consult supervisors and attorneys to put their findings in writing. If the evidence suggests the person might be American — even inconclusively — they should be released while the government decides.

Whether those safeguards were followed in Morales García's case remains unclear.

Still, the 2021 GAO investigation found that the protections were unevenly understood and applied. Some ICE officers had not been trained to follow the agency's own guidance, and neither ICE nor CBP reliably tracked every citizen that's been detained or removed, the report found. Agents are also not required to correct their databases if someone they investigated turned out to be a citizen.

On paper, it's the government's job to prove that someone is not a citizen. In reality, Stevens said, the burden often flips — a result, in part, of Supreme Court rulings that have given immigration authorities broad power and few judicial checks, she said.

Yet, what feels different now, Stevens said, is DHS's growing willingness to double down even after evidence of citizenship emerges.

"Information that's consistent with deportation is treated as accurate," she said. "And information that's inconsistent with deportation is treated as inaccurate and fraudulent."

Last year, 22-year-old Dulce Consuelo Diaz Morales spent 25 days in ICE custody while DHS challenged her Maryland birth certificate. Months later, she received a U.S. passport, and the government dropped its effort to deport her, the Baltimore Banner reported. In Florida, Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, remained jailed even after a judge verified that he was American, while DHS maintained that he had told officers he was undocumented, according to the Oklahoma Voice.

From Mexico, Morales García could do little more than wait while his attorneys tried to reconstruct the paper trail of his life. In May, they filed a federal lawsuit accusing federal, state and local officials of violating his constitutional rights and asking a judge to order the government to bring him home.

Three weeks after Morales García's attorneys sued, the government told a different story.

In a May 21 court filing, Justice Department attorneys said Morales García initially claimed citizenship and told a Border Patrol agent that he had entered the country with a birth certificate. But after the agent warned him that lying could bring criminal charges, they wrote, Morales García stated that he had been born in Zacatecas.

The DOJ denied that he was threatened or coerced, stating in court documents that he freely signed documents requesting a voluntary return to Mexico. It also pointed to Mexican records bearing another birth date, the spelling "Bryan" and an identity code associated with Zacatecas, Mexico.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Morales García's mother registered his birth in Mexico in 2004. The registrar, according to the family, entered a different date and changed "Brian" to "Bryan," a spelling more commonly used there. Having records in two countries — and discrepancies between them — is common among dual citizens, both Lincoln-Goldfinch and Stevens said.

After nearly five months — and a growing file of evidence — the Justice Department agreed to let Morales García return to the United States, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

On Aug. 30, after a bus ride north from Aguascalientes, Morales García found himself at the border once more. In his hands was the Colorado birth certificate his lawyers had spent months trying to make the government believe. This time, it was enough.

On the other side, his attorneys took him to Starbucks for coffee.

But coming back did not erase what had happened, Morales García said, alleging officers had judged him by how he looked and by the English he could not speak. He worried another traffic stop could end the same way.

"That fear will always be with me," he said in Spanish during a news conference. "It happened once and it can happen a second time."

His return did not end the lawsuit. Richard "Dicky" Grigg, one of his attorneys, said they plan to seek damages to keep other citizens from going through the same ordeal.

"They sent this man, a U.S. citizen, to Mexico, took four months of his life and then let him back in the United States when they realized they'd made a mistake," Grigg said. "To prevent this from happening in the future, we're going to do what we can to make sure government officials, state and federal, are held accountable and responsible."

Morales García's own plans are simpler. He wants to return to work and do what he came to the United States to do in the first place.

"Echarle ganas," he said — to keep going, keep working and keep giving it his all.

title: Texas Republican: ‘I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy’
description: Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally r...
fullText:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense's argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"I don't have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy," Gill said Friday on Fox News's "The Will Cain Show."

"I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered," he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy's defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family's Massachusetts home in 2023.

"You don't get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems," Gill said. "We've gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil."

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy's attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

"It's a shame. It's a horrible tragedy," Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. "She did a horrible, horrible thing."

"I guess they're going to go through another trial. It's too bad," he concluded.

title: Here is everything we learned from Texas A&M's 50-0 win over MO State
description: On Saturday, Texas A&M took on the Missouri State. Check out our top takeaways from the 50-0 shutout victory.
fullText:
No. 8 Texas A&M didn't look like the 8th-ranked team early in the first half of Saturday's season opener vs. Missouri State, as the revamped offensive line looked borderline horrific, allowing a handful of pressures and two sacks on starting quarterback Marcel Reed.

Third-year coach Mike Elko made the necessary changes that were noticeable as soon as halftime ended, while OL coach Adam Cushing also made adjustments to his rotation that produced a much better second-half performance, especially in the run game. Marcel Reed was nearly flawless, completing 21/30 for 233 yards and two touchdowns, deserving his spot on the bench late in the second half.

On the ground, WR Terry Bussey, sophomore running back Jamarion Morrow, and freshman RB Carsyn Baker scored touchdowns, led by Rueben Owens' 77 yards on 17 carries. Transfer wide receiver Isaiah Horton made his presence felt, recording a game-high 77 yards and a touchdown, continuing where he left off during the preseason.

Texas A&M's defense was elite, allowing 30 passing yards and 37 rushing yards for 67 total yards on the night, which is even more impressive after recording just one sack, while sophomore linebacker Noah Mikhail led the team with seven tackles. Right now, I fully expect the Aggie D to get even better as the season rolls on.

Earning its first shutout win since 1993, the Aggies left Kyle Field with a 50-0 victory, spurring plenty of takeaways before hosting Arizona State on Saturday. Here is everything we learned from Saturday's blowout win.

At 6'4" and 215 pounds, former Alabama wide receiver Isaiah Horton truly was the missing link to last season's productive receiver corps, but this season, Saturday's win proved that Horton was the cherry on top of what should be considered one of the deepest wide receiver rooms in the country.

Leading the game with 76 yards and his first touchdown of the season, Horton is just getting started, already becoming a favorite target for Marcel Reed on deep balls and red zone looks, while pairing well with Mario Craver, Ashton Bethel-Roman, and Terry Bussey. Expect Reed to heavily target Horton against Arizona's State on Saturday.

Texas A&M junior LB Daymion Sanford warmed up but did not play on Saturday, and based on how his fellow linebackers performed, it was a good move from Mike Elko to save his star defender for the rest of the season. Leading the game with seven tackles, sophomore LB Noah Mikhail was highly impressive, while transfer backer Ray Coney was second on the team with six tackles and half a TFL.

The combination of speed, size, and physicality, especially in the run game, helped limit Missouri State to 67 total yards, which is the lowest total allowed from an A&M defense in 30 years. Adding Sanford back into the lineup will make this unit one of the best in the SEC, especially if freshman Tamarion Watkins, who recorded two tackles and a TFL, continues to receive more playing time.

Texas A&M's offensive line was a disaster in the first half, allowing several early pressures and forcing Marcel Reed to use his legs, which was successful on nearly every attempt, but also resulted in two sacks. Junior Blake Ivy struggled during his first start at left guard, while senior center Mark Nabou committed multiple penalties.

Whatever adjustments Mike Elko and OL coach Adam Cushing made resulted in the Aggie O-line allowing zero sacks and giving Marcel Reed plenty of time to make his reads and deliver accurate throws, while opening up the running game, which produced 236 yards and three touchdowns.

The OL struggling this early is good timing for Elko and Cushing to make lineup changes, or simply fix the communication issues before hosting Arizona State, and especially before SEC play begins.

Texas A&M's run game exploded in the second half, as wide receiver Terry Bussey, sophomore running back Jamarion Morrow, and freshman back Carsyn Baker all scored touchdowns, paired with freshman KJ Edwards producing 44 yards on five carries for 8.8 yards per carry.

Rueben Owens led the room with 77 yards, but it's clear that Baker and Edwards are the most explosive options outside of Jamarion Morrow, and after the win, Mike Elko stated that both youngsters are "going to play a lot" moving forward.

With the new 5-for-5 rule taking effect this season, Mike Elko isn't just forced to play most of his freshmen, but will gladly do so if this level of play continues. Owens and Morrow will continue to lead the room, while Baker and Edwards provide elite depth.

After his best preseason performance yet, redshirt junior Marcel Reed made impressive throw after impressive throw on Saturday, showcasing his improved accuracy and touch, while layering several passes that proved his offseason was built around correcting his remaining mechanical issues.

Despite the poor O-line play in the first half, first-year OC Holmon Wiggins allowed Reed to use his legs, opening up the passing game, which led to Reed delivering red-zone strikes to Isaiah Horton and Mario Craver for his two touchdown throws before hitting the bench late in the second half, completing an efficient 21/30 for 233 yards and two touchdowns.

For the Aggies to have any legitimate shot at making it back to the College Football Playoff, Marcel Reed will need to continue elevating his game and playing with confidence in the pocket.

title: Texas A&M looks to end its College GameDay struggles in 2026
description: Texas A&M faces a long-standing struggle to win when ESPN's College GameDay visits College Station, losing to right the ship under HC Mike Elko.
fullText:
Texas A&M kicked off the 2026 regular season against Missouri State on Saturday night, and while starting the season off 1-0 was fully expected, one of third-year coach Mike Elko's remaining challenges that has haunted the program for 20-plus seasons resurfaced this week before the season opener, as ESPN's College GameDay's nine appearances in College Station have been disastrous.

Since 2000, Texas A&M is just 1-8 when College GameDay made its way to College Station, with the first loss coming against No. 1 Oklahoma 35-31, while the only win came during the 2016 season when the Aggies defeated visiting Tennessee 45-38 in double overtime, which happens to be one of the most exciting finishes in recent memory.

Since that victory, the Jimbo Fisher era has been equally disappointing after six seasons, while the lone College GameDay loss to Clemson during Fisher's first season at the helm was a game that could, and should have, gone the other way if it weren't for several avoidable performances.

During Mike Elko's inaugural season, Texas A&M's loss to rival Texas at the end of the 2024 season wasn't a shock given the talent differential, while the Aggies' first-round loss to Miami in the first round of the College Football Playoff was by far the most disappointing defeat with College GameDay in town.

When the lights are brightest, Texas A&M must respond if the Aggies want to be taken seriously as a program truly building and contending for national titles, and while the 2025 season was certainly a solid start, expectations are even higher in 2026. If College GameDay makes its way back to College Station, it's time to change the narrative.

title: Who is Indiana football’s backup quarterback? Meet Grant Wilson
description: Indiana football backup Grant Wilson has entered the game against North Texas. Here's what to know about the veteran:
fullText:
BLOOMINGTON — Indiana football backup quarterback Grant Wilson made his 2026 debut Saturday in the fourth quarter of his team's season opener.

Wilson's first game reps came with IU leading 45-16 over North Texas. He scored on the first snap. It was the first time he played since a Week 10 win over Maryland in 2025.

The veteran quarterback won the backup job for the Hoosiers in fall camp over Tyler Cherry. Here's what to know about Wilson:

More: IU's Curt Cignetti keeps sideline reporters on their toes. They wouldn't want it any other way

When Cignetti's staff landed in Bloomington, Wilson was a familiar name in the transfer portal.

The former Old Dominion starter faced off against Cignetti's JMU team in 2023 and nearly ended the program's 10-0 start. Wilson threw for 277 yards (26 of 36) and two touchdowns in the 30-27 loss.

Wilson threw a go-ahead score in the fourth quarter of the game that was overturned on replay.

More: Big Noon crew praises IU football's blueprint for developing transfer QBs

Wilson suffered a devastating arm injury during a Week 2 loss to East Carolina in 2024. He dislocated his elbow, tore a tendon in his tricep and another one in his wrist.

While rehabbing the injury after the season, Wilson received offers to compete for a starting job from Group of Five teams when he entered the transfer portal. Indiana also expressed interest in having him to Bloomington in what essentially amounted to a mentor role for the Mendoza brothers.

"It's hard to turn down Curt Cignetti," Wilson told The Herald-Times in 2025. "Just listening to his pitch and seeing what he did from Elon to JMU, the 2024 season. It's unreal, hard to deny the success he had."

More: Why Urban Meyer believes Indiana football has key advantage in quest for repeat titles

As IU's third-string quarterback, Wilson dedicated much of his energy to helping Fernando Mendoza and his brother. Wilson would spend extra time watching film with Fernando and offer him immediate feedback on reps during practice.

"He's like a full-time quarterback fundamental coach," Mendoza told The Herald-Times in 2025.

Then Indiana quarterbacks coach Chandler Whitmer appreciated Wilson's efforts as well.

"It's nice to have another voice in there that's aligned with what I'm teaching, and obviously in the meetings every single day and be another voice for Fernando as a peer," Whitmer said. "Grant has been great, I can't say enough good things."

More: How Indiana football QB Josh Hoover found his way back to Bloomington

Wilson wants to get into coaching, but he delayed those pursuits when the NCAA granted his waiver for a seventh season of eligibility. He returned to Bloomington and won the backup job over Tyler Cherry during fall camp.

"I would say Grant definitely has the edge for the number two," Cignetti said. "He's an experienced guy, and he's had a good camp. And Tyler's improved, too."

Wilson has thrown for 2,661 yards with 21 touchdowns and 11 interceptions in 18 games at the FBS level. At Fordham from 2021-22, he threw for 93 yards and two scores.

fullText:
For the first time since their 2025 Citrus Bowl loss to the Texas Longhorns, the Michigan Wolverines will be back on the football field this weekend. They'll be led for the first time by former Utah football coach Kyle Whittingham, but he's not the only fresh face coming from the Intermountain West.

All-American EDGE John Henry Daley is another of several Utah transplants. And after ending his 2025 campaign on a sour note with a ruptured Achilles, the senior transfer is expected to play in Michigan's season opener against Western Michigan at the Big House on Saturday.

At his first in-season press conference at the helm of the Wolverines on Monday, Whittingham described the standout pass rusher — who logged 48 tackles and 11.5 sacks in a slightly abridged year with the Utes — as "100% ready to roll."

While the excitement surrounding Daley's potential — and defensive coordinator Jay Hill's defense at large — is palpable in Ann Arbor, questions remain. Just over nine months have passed since Daley suffered his injury without contact during a Big 12 battle between Utah and Kansas State. Since then, the Wolverines have been careful to limit Daley's reps during fall camp.

Despite the caution surrounding Daley's situation, though, Whittingham and Hill appear bullish on his ability to play impactful football, with both coaches spotlighting physical improvements in his game.

On Monday, Whittingham said Daley is "probably more explosive and quicker than he's ever been." Hill echoed those sentiments later in the week and praised Michigan's staff for its handling of his injury.

"He's stronger than he's been. He's still coming off an injury, so … Coach [Lewis] Powell's done a great job of just monitoring that injury to where we've got to get him back, but we expect him to be full go," Hill told reporters during a Wednesday press conference.

"I've seen John Henry in person, and then I've played against him or coached against him. So, he's a really, really good player when he's fully healthy and going. And we expect him to be going."

Before his 2025 breakout, Daley split his previous two seasons with Utah and BYU. He logged just four tackles and a sack in 2024 with Utah after appearing in three games as a freshman for the Cougars the prior year.

As Hill seeks to integrate new players and old while also instituting a new — albeit familiar — defensive scheme, having the team's best players on the field and lineup consistency will be crucial. To that end, another key cog — safety Rod Moore — is expected to play in the opener as well.

Moore missed the entire 2024 season with an ACL injury, then aggravated it again early last season. The sixth-year senior and three-time Wolverines captain has 147 career tackles and 7 interceptions.

He and junior safety Chris Bracy will be counted on to anchor a Michigan secondary that Hill and cornerbacks coach Jernaro Gilford expect to be one of the nation's best.

title: Latino voter backlash puts Texas governor's race on Democrats' midterm map
description: BEEVILLE, Texas, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The makeup and toys on Valencia Macias' table are items people buy on impulse at discount stores.
fullText:
BEEVILLE, Texas, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The makeup and toys on Valencia Macias' table are items people buy on impulse at discount stores. But on a sweltering summer day in South Texas, she is trying to sell them to turn them into gas money, grocery money, student loan money: any kind of money.

With three young children, a job as a medical assistant and nursing classes at night, the 26-year-old ‌has little time for politics. But when Texas officials withdrew funding for the only after-school program available in her rural town of George West, politics became impossible to ignore.

Then, a TikTok video appeared: A Mexican American ‌woman on the screen, Gina Hinojosa, talked about the high cost of living and badly needed investments in Texas public education. Macias stopped scrolling.

"With everything just getting so expensive and the gas and everything, it's really hard to just make do," Macias said. Seeing a mother and a woman who ​looks like her, Macias made up her mind: "100%, she has my vote."

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, is trying to end an electoral drought that has defined Texas politics for a generation: no Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Her strategy hinges on persuading Latino voters like Macias that rising costs and strained public schools matter more than the cultural and immigration issues that have pulled many Latino voters toward Republicans in recent years.

Hinojosa said that means resisting the tendency to treat Latino voters as a distinct political constituency with separate priorities. Instead, she argues they are motivated by the same concerns as other Texans, including housing costs, schools and day-to-day expenses. So, her campaign delivers that message in Spanish to Latino audiences.

"We are as Texan and American as anyone," ‌she said in an interview in Austin. "Latinos are feeling the economic strain just like ⁠families all across this country and in Texas in a big way."

Her campaign tests whether Democrats can regain support among Latino voters by emphasizing pocketbook issues.

The test is whether it can overcome the political machine Republican Governor Greg Abbott has built over the last 12 years in office.

He has name recognition, President Donald Trump's endorsement and a vast support network that stretches beyond ⁠Texas. He has raised roughly $25.5 million between February and July, while Hinojosa raised about $6 million. Abbott holds more than a 22-to-1 cash-on-hand advantage, with $67.2 million to Hinojosa's $3 million, the latest campaign finance reports show.

Abbott spent years cultivating support in South Texas, regularly visiting heavily Latino border communities, building an extensive field operation in the Rio Grande Valley and making border security a centerpiece of his outreach.

Republican gains followed his sustained efforts to compete for Hispanic voters on issues including immigration, public safety and the economy.

Hinojosa's betting that the sharp drop in ​support ​for Trump and the party he leads will lead her to victory. State polls have consistently shown she's within striking distance of Abbott ​all year.

Abbott is still favored to win in the Republican-leaning state. Hinojosa would have ‌to break the three-decade Republican streak in the office. To stay in power, Abbott has turned to a Republican playbook portraying Hinojosa as out of step with his law-and-order agenda on the campaign trail.

"Governor Abbott is not taking the support of any voter — including Latino voters — for granted, which is why he is investing significant time and resources to earn votes in every community," Abbott's campaign press secretary Eduardo Leal said in a statement to Reuters.

Recent polling suggests Latino voters favor Hinojosa over Abbott. An August 2026 Emerson College Polling/Nexstar survey found Hispanic voters favored Hinojosa over Abbott by 17 percentage points and that 57% disapproved of Abbott's job performance. That same statewide poll, which surveyed 1,000 likely voters, showed Abbott leading Hinojosa 49% to 45% overall, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Abbott recently released an "affordability agenda" — including property tax cuts, housing reforms, lower electricity costs, expanded low-cost health insurance, a $25-a-month cap on certain prescription drugs, and more. His campaign says the measures will ‌help Texans offset rising living expenses.

"Latino voters care about the same issues that are important to all Texans: overhauling the property tax system, ​securing the border, putting dangerous criminals behind bars, and keeping Texas affordable," Leal said.

Samuel Aguero, 28, a Navy veteran, voted for Trump in 2024. ​But as a single father of two daughters, his top issue is education — he says Beeville's public schools ​need more state resources, and if Hinojosa offers specifics on improving them, he may back her instead.

"We have to have higher standards in school," he said. "Teachers should be paid a lot more, ‌like, a heck of a lot more."

Hinojosa may benefit from electoral tailwinds that eluded Beto ​O'Rourke and other statewide Democratic candidates before her.

Demographic trends have strengthened ​Democrats' long-held belief that Texas' growing Latino electorate could eventually reshape statewide politics. Texas now has about 6.5 million Latino eligible voters, roughly 1 million more than in the years leading up to Abbott's last reelection campaign.

But the key to Hinojosa's campaign is how many people actually turn out to vote. Nearly 4.5 million Texans voted in the Democratic and Republican primary elections in March, a recent midterm record.

Record participation, fueled by the high-profile ​Senate primary battles involving Attorney General Ken Paxton and State Representative James Talarico, could ‌offer Democrats a rare sign of momentum in a state where voter turnout has historically trailed the national average.

Still, voters like Dawn Barraza, 54, an eighth-grade schoolteacher in Victoria, Texas, want "change." At a monthly outdoor ​market in Beeville, Barraza said her family fares okay financially, but there's palpable frustration among Latinos in South Texas that Republicans are not addressing.

"They need to be standing up for our people here; it's high ​time everybody realizes that we're not going anywhere," she said.

His finale against Michigan became the exclamation point: Manning threw for 221 yards and two scores, rushed for 155 yards and two more touchdowns, and earned Citrus Bowl MVP honors in Texas' 41-27 win.

description: John Giusti and Brent Rosenkranz, from Texas, posted selfies from the Grand Canyon before devastating flash flooding swept through the area on Saturday.
fullText:
The two victims whose remains were found after flash flooding swept through the Grand Canyon were seen photographed on the same trip prior to the deadly incident.

The families of Texas chiropractor John Giusti, 46, and martial artist Brent Rosenkranz, 42, identified them as the two people whose bodies were recovered, according to Hannah Barricks, a liaison for the families. She told The Associated Press that a third friend, Timothy Smith, 53, went on the trip with them and remains missing as of late Monday.

All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas, and their families said they planned "several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together," the AP also reported. The men spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, the three families said in a joint statement released earlier Monday through Barricks.

The devastating flash flooding on Saturday, Aug. 29, happened along Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the Colorado River near Phantom Ranch. The area has a set of historic dormitories, a canteen and a campground that is a popular stopover for river rafters and people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other.

Grand Canyon Water Pipeline Damaged Again As Flooding Complicates Repairs

Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said searchers used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed rescuing during the deluge. By sunset Saturday, 45 people were rescued, and 37 others were evacuated Sunday.

Rangers referred to the park's permit system and checked vehicle license plates to track the number of missing people.

"As of right now, they have no reason to believe, from the tips we've been through so far, that there's anybody besides the one" missing person, Black said during a news conference Monday evening.

fullText:
The National Weather Service has issued a tropical storm and flood warning for the Houston and Galveston areas as Texas prepares for the storm's impact.

While the warning was issued on Aug. 31, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said in a social media post on Aug. 30 that Texas is monitoring the tropical storm in the Gulf set to impact the Houston area.

"We are already coordinating with electric power providers," Abbott said on social media. "If the system continues to develop, we will make announcements about emergency preparation, as needed."

The Texas Division of Emergency Management is also advising people to listen to local officials as the conditions develop and warnings are issued.

Here's what we know about the tropical storm and how to stay safe.

Bolivar, Crystal Beach and High Island have been placed under a Tropical Storm Warning by the weather service because the storm poses a threat to life and property.

As of a 10:10 a.m. warning notice on Aug. 31, the impact of wind is forecast to be limited, with 15-20 mph winds and gusts up to 40 mph and conditions being unfavorable for tornadoes. Storm surge is forecast to be limited, with localized storm surge possible up to two feet.

The real threat comes from flooding rains, as "moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and rescues," along with some road and bridge closures.

"Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially in usually vulnerable spots," read the warning. "Small streams, creeks, canals, and ditches overflow."

The weather service is advising people to heed any flood watches and warnings, leave immediately if evacuation orders are given and prepare now should conditions become hazardous.

The weather service placed Galveston and Houston under a flood warning until Wednesday morning, as periods of moderate to heavy rainfall associated with Potential Tropical Cyclone Five are expected to begin as early as late tonight and last into late Tuesday night/early Wednesday morning.

"3-5 inches with isolated amounts of 6-9 inches are expected with the highest totals occurring east of I-45," the warning stated. "Rainfall rates will exceed 3-4 inches per hour at times in the heaviest downpours, which can lead to flash flooding especially in urban and vulnerable areas."

The weather service advises residents to monitor later forecasts and watch for possible Flood Warnings; those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared to act if flooding develops.

The Texas Division of Emergency Management advises those experiencing a hurricane or tropical storm to do the following to stay safe:

If local officials say to evacuate, do so immediately.

Determine how best to protect yourself from high winds and flooding.

Take refuge in a designated storm shelter or an interior room for high winds.

Go to the highest level of the building if you are trapped by flooding. Do not climb into a closed attic as you may become trapped by rising flood water.

Do not walk, swim or drive through flood waters.

Remember: "Turn around. Don't drown," as just six inches of fast-moving water can knock people down, and one foot of moving water can sweep away a vehicle.

title: Plan to cut number of polling sites in a major Texas county draws protests as Senate race looms
description: A plan in one of Texas' largest counties to use dozens fewer polling locations than in previous years is drawing protests from Democrats who say the reductions could create confusion in the November m...
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A plan in one of Texas' largest counties to use dozens fewer polling locations than in previous years is drawing protests from Democrats who say the reductions could create confusion in the November midterm elections.

The proposal, set for a vote Tuesday, would reduce the number of polling locations across booming Tarrant County, which borders Dallas and includes Fort Worth. County officials say the plan would save resources by eliminating low-turnout sites, noting voters would still have more than 200 locations where they could cast ballots.

Texas' third-largest county is home to more than 2 million people and a key battleground in the U.S. Senate race between Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. On Sunday, Talarico urged the county to reject the proposal.

"The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don't want us to be able vote easily," Talarico said at a news conference.

If the plan is approved, Tarrant County would have 92 fewer polling locations on Election Day than it did during the 2022 midterms.

Closing polling locations in Texas is not a new trend, county elections officials say. The trend has been accelerated by an embrace of countywide voting sites and the difficulty in recruiting poll workers. Other Texas counties have also considered or already reduced the number of polling locations for November while some have added more.

"We're clearly not trying to suppress the vote," Rep. Matt Shaheen, the Republican chairman of the House Elections Committee, said of polling site reductions in Texas. "That's a silly accusation."

Tarrant County Elections Administrator Clint Ludwig has said the reductions would allow the county to eliminate locations that serve few people.

Locations near bus stops that complied with federal accessibility laws were prioritized to remain open, according to a county statement. Officials said the average distance between Election Day sites under the plan was 1.5 mile (2.4 kilometers).

"All of this is accomplished without the wasteful practice of placing polling sites directly across the street from one other," said Tarrant County Judge Tim O'Hare, a Republican and the county's top administrator.

Spokespeople for Paxton did not respond to emails seeking comment.

Texas law lets each of the state's 254 counties decide how many polling places to use. Tarrant County adopted countywide voting in 2019 but didn't immediately begin reducing the number of polling locations.

On Friday, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union joined voting rights groups in signing a letter urging the county to reject the proposal, saying the closures would be strongly felt in areas with high percentages of minority voters. About a third of the county's residents are Hispanic, and about 19.2% are Black, according to Census data.

Bastrop County Elections Administrator Kristin Miles, whose county is outside Austin, said reducing the number of polling sites could make sense, depending on how heavily they are used. Miles noted that there would be little point, for instance, in opening sites in rural areas that may only serve a handful of voters throughout the day.

Carol Raburn, who worked the March primaries as an election judge in Tarrant County, called the proposal a form of voter suppression.

"Because what happens when people don't have a convenient place to go vote that's not too far away from where they are, where they live? They just don't go vote because they've made it so difficult," she said.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Republicans ready for ‘very hasty’ ‘Trump-a-palooza’ convention in Texas
description: The Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first-of-its-kind midterm convention has been cloaked in mystery until a few weeks ago. Details are finally emerging about what’s expected to be a two-day pep...
fullText:
The Republican National Committee's (RNC) first-of-its-kind midterm convention has been cloaked in mystery until a few weeks ago. Details are finally emerging about what's expected to be a two-day pep rally to bolster hype and encourage Republicans to get out the vote in November amid President Trump's shrinking approval rate.

But some Republicans are quietly frustrated that the event came together so fast and at such a high price tag for lawmakers: House members are reportedly expected to contribute $25,000 to attend.

A GOP operative told The Hill that while Trump has touted the convention for a year, candidates and incumbents have not had long to plan.

"Lot of things made this very hasty that didn't need to happen," the operative said. Trump announced at the end of June that the convention would be in Dallas on Sept. 9 and 10.

The midweek convention also conflicts with the first two NFL games of the season and bumps against the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, raising questions about whether the "Trump-a-palooza" will get enough airplay to justify the expense.

And while primetime addresses from Trump and Vice President Vance could gin up excitement as Texas Republicans defend their toss-up Senate seat, the convention risks pulling candidates in other states off the campaign trail during a critical summer stretch.

"I think the big question on people's minds is whether or not this is helpful," said Joshua Blank, research director for the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, pointing to the program's polls that show Trump's approval rating underwater in the state.

Blank also looked back to 2018, when Democrats were rallying around Beto O'Rourke in his campaign to oust Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas). Trump, then in his first term, visited Texas to boost Cruz, but "most analyses after the fact tended to indicate that that visit didn't really help Cruz," he said.

"It raises the question of whether the timing is somewhere between ill-conceived or just not conceived at all," Blank added of the event scheduling. "This may be convenient for some, but it doesn't seem to be necessarily timed for maximum impact. It seems more like a reaction to concerns about enthusiasm among Republican voters. It's more of a reaction than it is a clear plan."

But Texas Republican consultant Brendan Steinhauser contended that "it's a net positive" for the GOP in Texas and beyond.

"It's two days. It's not two weeks … so you're not really taking away from anything else," he said. "Texas is indeed competitive, and this makes all the sense in the world to me," he said. "As long as it's a net positive financially, and they make use of the time and deliver a message, then I think it's a good thing."

Texas Republican strategist Vinny Minchillo argued that "people are digging really hard to find problems with the event," which he sees as a good opportunity to rev up the the GOP base in Texas as they look toward a Senate race that's "much tighter than anybody would really like on the Republican side."

"Certainly, conflicting with an NFL game early in the season is going to be tough," Minchillo said, but he argued that the conflict won't eclipse the convention's purpose as a "rally-the-troops event and an opportunity for fundraising."

"The people who want to watch the president are going to watch the president, and maybe the people who want to watch the NFL game are just going to record the president and watch him later," he added.

The major news networks have not said whether they will show coverage of the convention. A spokesperson for Fox News confirmed the network would broadcast some coverage, but the details have yet to be announced. About 20,000 people are expected to attend, according to John Hiller, White House aide and the CEO of the convention's organizing board.

Meanwhile, Dallas's city agencies are quickly preparing to secure the event. The Dallas Police Department (DPD) held a press conference with officials from the FBI and Secret Service Thursday afternoon, confirming that security needs would cost the city $1.8 million.

"The city is also actively evaluating reimbursement and grant opportunities and will pursue all eligible funding sources to help offset the costs to Dallas taxpayers," City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert said. "At the same time, reimbursements do not necessarily determine whether we provide necessary public safety services."

Deputy Police Chief Devon Palk said people will experience public transit and road closures as well as an increased law enforcement presence, including officers from other agencies that are not the DPD. Palk and Bizor Tolbert both said they expect protests related to the convention.

The cost comes after Bizor Tolbert announced spending restrictions this spring as the city veered toward a potential budget shortfall of more than $30 million for the fiscal year.

"We've got a city that's got budget problems, and the city of Dallas has a lot of financial issues. So $2 million is not an insignificant amount of money for them to spend," Minchillo said. "But that's what it costs to bring in these big events."

Dallas Mayor Eric Johnson, a longtime Democrat who switched to the GOP in 2023 and now helms the Republican Mayors Association, has said hosting the landmark midterm event is a "tremendous honor." Dallas is the largest U.S. city with a Republican mayor.

The RNC has announced 109 items and speakers for the two-day event, most of which are to be announced. Vance is set to give a keynote on the first night, and Trump will close out the second night.

title: Mike Elko eyes 'winning plays' for Texas A&M in 2026
description: Mike Elko aims to fix Texas A&M's playoff woes by refining Marcel Reed's role and strengthening the defense, needing more "winning plays" this season.
fullText:
Playing "winning football" sounds vague on the surface, and heading into Mike Elko's third season at the helm, it's clear that the program is in the right direction, but back-to-back losses to Texas and Miami in the first round of the College Football Playoff were the antithesis of what we saw throughout the 2025 season.

This starts and ends with redshirt junior quarterback Marcel Reed, who threw four of his career-high twelve interceptions in both losses while seemingly playing with less confidence compared to his past performances, resulting in poor decision-making; former OC Collin Klein's decision to use fewer RPO looks and keep Reed in the pocket also deserves some blame.

Under first-year offensive coordinator Holmon Wiggins, the expectation is that Marcel Reed will return to utilizing his dual-threat skill set more often, getting outside the pocket, especially on play action where he has thrived since becoming the full-time starter. Equipped with one of the best wide receiver rooms in the country, Reed's improvement this preseason should lead to another jump in consistent play.

However, the defense allowed nearly 400 rushing yards against Texas and Miami last season, a huge contributing factor in both losses that wasn't based on personnel, aside from a lack of size at linebacker, which has been addressed this offseason.

During Thursday's press conference, Mike Elko said taking another step toward making "winning plays" in key moments has been a clear focus, starting with finishing strong every practice, while his team's mental makeup will be tested throughout the nine-game SEC schedule.

"We got to continue to be the team that steps up and makes those winning plays in those moments, and that's what we did in those games… That's what we didn't do in the playoff game."

"The more parity sets in, which it clearly is, and the more that the top comes down a little bit and the bottom comes up… It's going to come down to winning plays."

Situations where Marcel Reed is dropping back in 12 personnel and needing to make perfect throws in tight windows must be avoided, if possible, to avoid placing added pressure; this starts with a strong run game, which will open up play-action looks and allow the Aggies' wide receivers to make plays after the catch.

title: Study conclude social media algorithms negatively influence users mental health
description: | While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health. Dr. Alva Tang, assistant professor of psychology in the School of Behavioral […]
fullText:
While social media algorithms have become excellent at matching a user’s viewing habits with targeted, personalized content, psychologists at The University of Texas at Dallas have determined that these algorithms may have a negative influence on a user’s mental health.

Dr. Alva Tang, assistant professor of psychology in the School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences, is corresponding author of a proof-of-concept study published online June 25 in Computers in Human Behavior that explores the links between algorithm-recommended content, how that content is processed by the brain and symptoms of depression.

Get the latest news and events delivered to your inbox.

In the study, 60 young adults with an average age of 20 were assessed via validated anxiety and depression scales. They then watched two sets of videos: one of personally recommended videos from their own Instagram or TikTok accounts, which were further categorized for content types; the other of generalized trending videos. Brain activity was recorded using EEG to measure frontal alpha asymmetry — a well-established measure of emotional processing and motivation.

“In frontal alpha asymmetry, dominance on the left represents more positive emotional processing,” Tang said. “Dominant right-sided activity is usually related to more negative processing and withdrawal-related behaviors.

“Instead of after-the-fact reflections, we looked at real-time emotion processing and documented reactions to watching personalized recommendations. In that regard, this study is novel. Prior research on this has been based on survey questions and self-reports. We are reporting what the study participants are looking at and how they are affected by what their feeds serve them.”

The study accounted for total screen time as a confound, or outside factor, which is used in the majority of research on this subject. First author Carole Leung, a doctoral student in cognition and neuroscience, explained that screen time might have weak relations with mental health because that time is not uniformly negative.

“It’s not just about how much time you spend on social media,” Leung said. “What the algorithm recommends to you matters, too. The emotional content in your personalized feed is linked to your brain’s real-time emotional responses and to depressive symptoms.”

Dr. Stacie Warren, associate professor of psychology and a co-author of the study, emphasized the immediacy of the neuroimaging being performed.

“EEG is a real-time processing measure of brain activity within milliseconds,” she said. “Combining brain activity measures with their own reporting on depressive symptoms gives us an objective measure to evaluate what happens as people engage in their algorithmically selected social media.”

The study results confirmed that participants with more depressive symptoms are provided recommendations that lean more depressive, and their brain activity — as determined by frontal alpha asymmetry — is characteristic of depression. This is distinct from their brain activity while watching videos that are trending generally.

“What we’re finding is that if you’re already feeling depressed, then the algorithms reflect that. Continued engagement reinforces this negative feedback loop,” Warren said. “Participants bring in their own phones; we are not selecting videos for them. It’s a new take on understanding how social media consumption affects people.”

The most common category of videos recommended to young adults concerns social relationships, either romantic or friendships. Tang said researchers are finding that the feelings participants displayed could impact the apps’ recommendations.

“If you’re more depressed, you’re more likely to be exposed to a video showing an argument or conflict,” she said. “Positive videos would be about friends supporting each other, for instance. There are videos we classify as neutral as well — those lacking emotional connotation.”

Viewing fewer positive social relationship videos also was associated with relative right frontal alpha asymmetry, or more negative feelings.

“Depressed individuals have a tendency to focus on negative things, dismissing the positive things they encounter,” Warren said. “If you’re depressed and you keep on scrolling, you will encounter fewer positive videos.”

Researchers hope to highlight ways to develop healthy social media engagement behaviors so that negative mood isn’t amplified. The main intervention now is educating people on how to engage with social media more critically and effectively.

“We are teaching teenagers who frequently use TikTok and Instagram how to curate positive content while limiting the negative by following and interacting with the right creators,” Tang said. “If they are tired of their feeds, an account can be set back to default, providing brand-new recommendations. From there, you can reteach the app what interests you.”

Parents also can be more aware of how algorithms influence mood, but limiting teens’ time on social media won’t teach them how to respond in a useful or adaptive way.

“Two years ago, the guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics was to reduce screen time,” Tang said. “These days, if you tell your teenager not to go on their phone, it’s like you’re taking away their life. That’s not going to work.”

Researchers are now collecting data on a cohort of teens ages 13 to 16 for a potential long-term study to understand the emotional effects of algorithm suggestions over time.

Other UT Dallas-affiliated contributors to the current study include Lucie H. Nguyen BS’25, an incoming medical student at Dell Medical School at UT Austin; former UT Dallas research assistant Christina Vlahakos, now a graduate student at Northwestern University; and Dr. Carlos Busso, now at Carnegie Mellon University.

This research was supported by a 2025 Social Sciences Seed Grant from UT Dallas and a Behavioral Health Research Award from the University of North Texas’ Center for Psychosocial Health Disparities Research.

title: ICE officer charged in Minneapolis shooting released in Texas after immediate extradition rejected
description: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday, after a judge ref...
fullText:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday, after a judge refused to order his return to Minnesota.

Christian Castro was released at the break of dawn from a detention center in Brownsville. He motioned his hand toward a few camera operators and a reporter crowding around him and quickly got into an SUV that drove off.

A day earlier, U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that said he couldn't prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro or order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro's arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota's Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remained in custody in Brownsville, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro had to be released after 90 days of detention, which was Thursday.

Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee to Mexico.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro's release or to order his return to Minnesota.

Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that's still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a "fugitive" under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said.

The judge wrote in Wednesday's order that the court couldn't yet step in.

"The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication," the order read. "Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred."

The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision.

Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

After the judge's decision, Ellison posted online that the Texas governor had an obligation to extradite Castro. And by refusing to extradite him, "Greg Abbott is turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals."

"You guys are such bad lawyers. You showed up unprepared, uninformed & unpersuasive," Abbott wrote online. "You don't know the law & it showed."

The Texas governor accused Minnesota of refusing to enforce immigration laws and threatened to send immigrants in the future to their state as he did with New York City, when thousands were released into Texas under President Joe Biden's administration.

A message seeking reaction from Ellison was sent to his office Thursday.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that "the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication."

Valerie Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this story.

title: New Texas poll shows tight Senate race, GOP pulling ahead for governor
description: Talarico leads Paxton 42-39 in the new UT/Texas Politics Project poll. Abbott leads Hinojosa in the governor's race, and data center opposition holds.
fullText:
Just over two months out from Election Day, a new Texas poll found three notable results: the candidates remain statistically tied in the U.S. Senate race, Republicans are pulling ahead in the governor's race, and Texans are united in their disdain for data centers.

A new University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll, published Aug. 25, finds 42% of Texas voters preferring Democrat state Rep. James Talarico and 39% planning to vote for Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the hotly contested U.S. Senate race in Texas.

Meanwhile, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott leads his Democratic challenger, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, 45% to 40%.

But the issue uniting Texans is their opposition to data centers: 57% said they oppose building a data center in their community, while 30% expressed support.

Here's a deep look at what the poll says on each topic.

The poll was conducted among 1,200 self-reported registered voters between Aug. 5 and 13 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points or 3.47% adjusted for weighting.

In a previous Texas Politics Project poll in June, Paxton led Talarico by a percentage point within the poll's margin of error, 43% to 42%, with 84% of Republicans saying they would support Paxton if the election were held then.

The August poll shows that Talarico leads within the poll's margin at 42%, with Paxton at 39%, Libertarian Ted Brown at 3% and 14% expressing no preference.

Talarico is consolidating Democratic support at 91%, while 79% of Republicans have expressed their commitment to Paxton. Among independents, 37% prefer Talarico, 11% prefer Paxton, and 43% express no preference.

Previous polling showed movement toward Democrats, but the Texas Politics Project August poll shows the trend has reversed.

Abbott leads Hinojosa, 45% to 40%, with the remaining 3% preferring Libertarian Pat Dixon, 2% choosing an unspecified "someone else," and 10% unable to express an opinion.

Hinojosa is still keeping the race in the single digits, closer than Democrat Beto O'Rourke's final 11-point loss to Abbott in 2022.

Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (42%) leads Democratic state Rep. Vikki Goodwin (35%) by seven points.

Republican Attorney General state Sen. Mayes Middleton (40%) leads Democratic state Sen. Nathan Johnson (35%) by five points.

Republican Comptroller Don Huffines (40%) leads Democratic state Sen. Sarah Eckhardt (34%) by six points.

A majority of Texans, 57%, said they oppose building a data center in their community, while only 30% expressed support and 14% had no opinion, according to the Texas Politics Project August poll.

This is the second consecutive poll from the Texas Politics Project to report the same findings, as its June poll showed 29% supported and 56% opposed local data center construction.

Breaking it down by political party,

Republicans remain closely divided: 45% support, 43% oppose.

Democrats strongly oppose: 75% oppose — with 59% saying they strongly oppose, 15% support.

Independents oppose: 54% oppose, 19% support.

Among rural voters, 25% expressed support, while 60% opposed — with 44% strongly opposing the construction of data centers. Suburban Texans mirror the same feelings.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro's arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota's Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro's release or to order his return to Minnesota.

Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that's still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a "fugitive" under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said.

The judge wrote in Wednesday's order that the court can't yet step in.

"The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication," the order read. "Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred."

The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision.

Ellison said in a statement that his office would keep litigating the case but didn't specify what it would do next.

"I respectfully but strongly disagree with the court's order, which nonetheless acknowledges that Christian Castro is a flight risk, that Minnesota will be harmed if he is allowed to flee to Mexico, and that Governor Abbott's consideration of Minnesota's extradition request is of 'an atypically long duration' — to say the least," Ellison said in a statement.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, whose office handles prosecutions in Minneapolis, said at a new conference that Abbott was unfairly harboring the former ICE agent.

"If Christian Castro walks out of the door of the jail tomorrow and disappears into Mexico, it will be the fault of one person: Governor Greg Abbott," Moriarty said.

Abbott's press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, welcomed the ruling and said it was the governor's duty to carefully consider the merits of extradition requests.

"Today's order rebuffs Minnesota's efforts to conscript federal courts into commandeering the authority of Governor Abbott's office," Mahaleris said in a statement.

Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that "the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication."

title: Evacuations ordered as wind-whipped Ross Fire in Texas explodes to 50,000 acres
description: Firefighters are battling numerous wildfires threatening homes in the West.
fullText:
A wind-whipped grass fire ignited on Monday near Fort Worth, Texas, rapidly spreading overnight to 50,000 acres and triggering evacuations, officials said.

The Ross Fire in Palo Pinto County, Texas, which has also shut down a highway, is the latest in a series of wildfires across the West and Northwest, and came just as fire crews in Nevada were making progress in battling a massive fire near Reno that has destroyed or damaged more than 50 homes and prompted 42,000 evacuations.

The Ross Fire was just 5% contained on Tuesday morning as it spread north into neighboring Jack County, where more people have been advised to evacuate, officials said.

"Firefighters are prioritizing life safety and structure protection, while working to establish containment lines where conditions safely allow," the Texas A&M Forest Service said in a statement on Tuesday.

The Ross Fire started about 1:30 p.m. local time on Monday near the town of Palo Pinto, about 60 miles west of Fort Worth, and grew to 18,000 acres in just 12 hours, according to the Palo Pinto Emergency Services Department.

"Residents are strongly encouraged to leave the area now, particularly those who may need additional time or assistance evacuating," the Palo Pinto County Sheriff said in a social media statement issued Monday night.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Meanwhile, firefighters are gaining the upper hand on a massive brush fire that ignited over the weekend in the hills in Northern Nevada near Reno, destroying numerous homes and prompting the evacuation of 42,000 people over the past few days, officials said.

At a press briefing Tuesday afternoon, Nevada fire officials said the fire has burned more than 15,000 acres, destroyed at least 47 homes and seriously damaged eight others. At least seven people, including three first responders, have been injured in the blaze, officials said.

Containment lines around the Hawk Fire on Monday went from zero to 27%, and fire crews appear to have stopped the blaze from reaching the community of Somersett in northwest Reno, fire officials said at a news conference earlier Tuesday.

Firefighters report progress in battle against massive Hawk Fire in Nevada

Evacuation orders have been lifted in some areas, and the number of people under evacuation has been reduced to 23,000 from 42,000.

The Hawk Fire is suspected to be human-caused, but officials said investigators have yet to determine if it was intentionally or accidentally set.

In the state of Washington, 15 large uncontained fires have consumed 800,000 acres, officials said.

The largest fires currently in Washington are the Little Giant Fire in Chelan County, which has consumed more than 142,000 acres, and the Sinlahekin Fire in  Okanogan County, which has burned more than 155,000 acres.

'Nightmare situation': At least 700 structures destroyed in Washington wildfires

The Sinlahekin Fire, which was started by a lightning strike on July 26, was 55% contained on Tuesday, officials said. The Little Giant Fire, also sparked by a lightning strike on July 15, was 15% contained on Tuesday, officials said.

Both fires are burning in remote areas of the state and are not threatening homes, officials said.

"Washington is comfortably in the third-worst fire season from an acres burned perspective since 2015," Thomas Kyle-Milward, a spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, told ABC affiliate station KOMO in Seattle.

Kyle-Milward said this wildfire season has been particularly challenging for firefighters, noting that the state has had multiple fires over 100,000 acres.

A series of fires earlier this month in Spokane caused $1 billion in damage, including destroying more than 800 homes, the Spokane County Assessor announced last week.

A 37-year-old man was arrested and charged with starting the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 1, one of three major wildfires that became known as the Spokane Complex Fire.
